utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom and just outside the courtroom assisting us. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before I'll ask the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, I would like to ask a few questions which might have some relevance for the -- this might have some relevance for decisions taken at a later stage about whether or not the Defence is instructed -- will be instructed to start to cross-examine the witness or not to start to cross-examine the witness. Mr. Tieger, could you explain a bit more, and I conveyed to the Defence that I instructed our staff to already try to find out whether anything was known about it. Could you say a bit more about the recently disclosed material. I do understand that when we started approximately with an estimate of approximately 25.000 pages that it was later brought to 1600 up to 2000 pages [sic]. To what extent was that material new to the Defence? And of course, you'll have an opportunity to respond, Mr. Stewart, if we have received answers from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I undertook an analysis of the material that was disclosed last night. I can go over the methodology, if the Court wishes, but the bottom line is that I estimate that between 200 and 400 pages were new.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, is that something you would consider to be a proper estimate?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have no idea, Your Honour, to be frank, because, after all, this figure has just been presented to me. I haven't been asked to do that exercise. But as far as new material is concerned, it perhaps is necessary to be clear about what -- what's within the definition of new.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll ask Mr. Tieger what he -- how he identified what is new and what's not new.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I attempted to go about it in a couple of ways, Your Honour. First of all, I printed out all of the documents. I didn't have time to go through all of them. I went through the first couple hundred of the 380 documents that were disclosed. Of those, I found that approximately 70 had been previously tendered through other witnesses. And according to disclosure logs, about 90 per cent of them, the ones that I had looked at, had been previously disclosed, often times repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give us any indication -- when I'm talking about new, well, let's say, I think for the scheduling of Mr. Mandic to testify in November was first raised early October. I think it was on the 13th of October that the matter first appeared. Was there -- if you're talking about old and new, would you consider old to be disclosed, well, before early October of this year?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, is there any need to further -- I just want to make a separation between the time period which -- prior to the first indications of scheduling Mr. Mandic for November and after that period of time. Do you have any observations to make on the answer given by Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I have a simple observation, Your Honour, which is this: That we did receive some substantial disclosure of an enormous number of documents on the 29th of June of this year, and I believe - I'm simply telling Your Honours as much as I know and understand - I believe that a significant amount of this material was included in that disclosure. So in that technical sense, it's not new. And, Your Honour, I entirely accept, we've accepted throughout this case, that a very great deal of material is not new in the absolute technical sense, that it has been disclosed to the Defence at some point since the case began. We say in the end that's not actually the test. But in answer to Your Honour's relatively narrow question, but Your Honour will be aware that when we received that disclosure on the 29th of June, first of all, Mr. Mandic was not a witness. And secondly, there was no question of any portion of that disclosure being identified as attributable or relevant to Mr. Mandic. So we -- it's -- I don't know off the top of my head. It was a very large amount of material, Your Honour. So I'm just answering Your Honour's relatively narrow question in those relatively narrow terms, that as far as I'm aware, yes, in that technical sense of the word "new," a great deal of this material is not new. I haven't checked the figures and gone through the material in the same way. But, Your Honour, there's a lot more to be said, may I simply observe, on the question of preparedness to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I would first like to put some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. Well, that's my answer as best as I can do. I appreciate it's not a very wonderful, detailed, informative answer, but I'm doing my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's at least a short answer, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Tieger, how much of that material will be tendered in evidence through this witness, approximately? I'm not asking for exact page numbers, but approximately. Because if these were 1.600 pages, does that mean that we can expect all 1.600 to be tendered or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That is not the case. And I think it's -- there are approximately 60 exhibits that will be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Amounting to approximately how many pages, just a rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would estimate 200.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What was the reason to disclose or even re-disclose material that would not be tendered through this witness exactly in this, well, let's say the last few days before the witness was called?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, those materials, first, I wouldn't describe them as being tendered in the last few days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the list Mr. Stewart gave us is about -- ends on the 22nd of November, I think. You've seen that list, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Those are re-disclosure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a couple of days, but, well, relatively close to the day of the appearance of the witness in this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would say it follows under the rubric of no good deed goes unpunished, Your Honour. We try to disclose to the Defence the exhibit list, and the final disclosure in fact was the history of the disclosure process, which included all the material from the beginning down to the narrower portions that were received at the end. I had hoped that had been made clear in the earlier discussion. Perhaps it was not. But we progressively narrowed it down. As for some of the material that had been previously disclosed being disclosed at the beginning, Mr. Stewart has indicated to the Court earlier that there is a lot of material in this case. There is. It seemed to us it would be helpful to identify -- since we had been through the process of preliminarily looking at the material to share with him the benefit of some of that preliminary review and winnow down initially from the vast body of material, through which he might want to look, and might be faster at it than us, but indicate the results of what we had found, and at least exclude some of the universe of materials through which he might otherwise be looking. I think I indicated that earlier as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because it appears from the list provided to us by Mr. Stewart that the exhibit list and the final exhibit list, I think, were both given to the Defence on the 22nd of November. Is that a correct understanding? That's at least what I read from that list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can check the history, but I know the preliminary exhibit list was distributed considerably earlier than November 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm trying to be helpful. It was on that note. Could I just say, Your Honour, we tried to make it consistently clear and repeat it that our position on this does not involve an attack or criticism on the Prosecution. That remains the position. I want Mr. Tieger through the Trial Chamber to understand that. But, Your Honour, so far as the exhibit list is concerned, it was on that schedule which I handed up a few days ago. We were provided with a first exhibit list, or draft exhibit list, whatever it was, including Rule 66 material as well, on the 15th of November. We had another one later that day, two at different times on the 17th, and then two on the 22nd. So that was the history of those, well, presumably, continually refined lists, ending up with the last one on the 22nd, which was, well, Monday this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I should have looked better at the list, where I mentioned the two disclosures of the exhibit list on the 22nd, it now turns out that there were earlier ones on the 15th of November, two of them, one on the 17th of November. Are there considerable changes in the 15th of November list and the 22nd of November list? Perhaps we could ask Mr. Tieger, because he certainly has updated -- will have updated them. I mean, it's just adding one or two or taking out one or two or --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's deleting, for the most part, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Deleting for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Primarily, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to give an opportunity to briefly address the matter, Mr. Stewart. If you could do that, come to the core, to the problem right away. First of all, try to do that in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can do one of two things. I can assert and tell Your Honour that the Defence is simply not ready to proceed with Mr. Mandic. We are simply unable to have dealt with the volume of material. I can assert that in 30 seconds. Your Honour, if I am to detail what we have received, to put it in proper context and explain to Your Honour, that is bound to take more than five minutes. There is no way I can do it in five minutes. It also gets into that rather difficult area, Your Honour, where, first of all, we would not be very happy to be disclosing to the public and then potentially -- because after all the witness is a member of the public for these purposes. Nobody can stop the witness from finding out what's said in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. If you would prefer to deal with it in private session, we'll now turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, beyond that, there's a question -- I'm not asking for that immediately, Your Honour, until we get to that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just offering it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I know. Indeed, Your Honour. I'm very grateful for the offer and, in relation to that particular point, would accept it. But before we do go into private session, I have the further point, Your Honour, that beyond what we would not be particularly happy to have -- well, not be happy at all to have disclosed to the public in that way, there are points which we're not particularly happy to disclose to the Prosecution either. Why -- I ask rhetorically, why should we, Your Honour, in explaining about cross-examination and cross-examination material, why should we advertise everywhere we're going to the Prosecution, who haven't even finished examining the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. On the other hand, I take it that both the Prosecution and Defence would like to know whether we'll -- whether the Chamber will follow the Defence in its assertion that it cannot cross-examine, or at least not start to cross-examine the witness. If that decision would be taken at the end of the examination-in-chief of this witness, that might well be early next week, because I understand from the Prosecution that it would take today and perhaps one or two hours next week, and that's more or less in accordance with the scheduling. But then, of course, there is a risk, Mr. Stewart, that if the Chamber would then decide that you should start your cross-examination, that you'll not -- well, at least you know it only then and you would not know it by the end of this day. But I leave it up to you. If you say, now, "I'd rather not discuss this matter any further, apart from asserting that you're not ready to cross-examine the witness and leave it to the Chamber to decide whether or not the Defence is invited to at least start the cross-examination, then leave it --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have, as Your Honour very sympathetically recognises. Of course we would have a strong preference for knowing today, because we've got plenty else that we can usefully do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then what is your suggestion? Would it be acceptable for the Prosecution to hear -- because I do understand that to lay the whole of the cross-examination on the table now might not be something that -- well, that still could influence the line of examination-in-chief of this witness. So we're a bit in a dilemma.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I try and short-circuit it, because I mention that as a possible problem. But it may not be a practical problem, because, Your Honour, what I -- there's a limited area and Your Honour says, "lay the whole of the cross-examination," it follows from what I said. That's the one thing I'm not in a position to do. But the -- but Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to slow down, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My enthusiasm to have us move on, Your Honour, I will now curb or restrain. Your Honour, what I propose to do, then, if I may, it will be a while until I got to the point where I was getting to something so sensitive that I was especially nervous about the Prosecution hearing it. I can indicate to Your Honours, but preferably in private session, for the reasons I've given, the scale and nature of the material for quite a long time before I get to the point where I don't wish Mr. Tieger's and other's ears to hear it. It's probably not a difficulty, and it may be, Your Honour, that I will have convinced the Trial Chamber before I need to get into that sensitive area of the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much will you need if we now turn into private session to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As best I can do, Your Honour, from the notes I've got and my knowledge of the material, I may have to consult Ms. Cmeric from time to time, maybe something like 15 minutes or so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, we'll turn into private session, and you'll have 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again. Let me ask one final thing. If the Chamber, in order to get a better impression on one -- at least one of the issues raised, that is, the new material, new Article 68 material, the 20 items of which 12 are new, would the parties oppose against Chamber looking at it, not for its content, but mainly in order to get an impression of what type of material that is? Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I feel more comfortable if I had a chance to look at it myself. Most of the items are in B/C/S. I'm not quite sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You told us. Only two were in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. So I don't know exactly how it's going to work, Your Honour. But I'm sure Your Honour understands that first observation I just made in response to what you just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, would you -- yes, I do understand that you'd rather first look at it yourself, but at the same time you're not in a position to do so because you can't read it. Mr. Tieger, what would be your position? Even without reading it, I mean perhaps even better without reading it. You can get an impression of what type of material that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't have an objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Mandic, I apologise for not -- for continuing with procedural issues when you entered the courtroom. Thank you very much for your patience. The same to you, Mr. Tomic. Mr. Mandic, may I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Tieger will now resume his examination-in-chief. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At the conclusion of yesterday, we had listened to an intercepted telephone conversation which was P292, KID 31469. I'd ask if the transcript could be placed in front of Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think -- we received the document. It's the 25th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, just to remind you, that was the conversation between you and Mr. Krajisnik on the 25th of June, 1992, during which he raised the issue of Milos Savic's brother and his family. If I could ask you to turn to the second page of the B/C/S transcript, the transcript in front of you, and also the second page of the English translation. You state to

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "Mr. President." And then he responds, "Yes, that first part has been ocistiti [phoen]. It was done today." Do you recall, Mr. Mandic, what area, what part was being referred to in that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what did you mean when you said, if you recall, that it had been "ocistiti," either mopped up or cleansed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if we were referring to some barricades or obstacles that were up there near Lukavica. I can't remember what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know who Mr. Krajisnik was referring to when he said, "Did they leave?"

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably referred to the removal of some obstacles so that people had free passage both ways. I believe that it was an obstacle in question, but I cannot remember what it was exactly about. Because it's obvious that people were moving around and crossing over.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we believe -- when I say we, it's the sort of royal we, because it's Ms. Cmeric who has this belief. We believe that the translation, "did they leave" is perhaps not the fully correct translation of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I suppose that points out again the wisdom of asking after the intercept is played whether it's correct, but if that wasn't identified before, I guess we need to know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, we're now at the point where it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact, the human limitations of picking up such a large number of difficulties on these intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Cmeric would you please read that part so that we can verify whether the -- and you're now reading which box of the second page? Let me just try to locate it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's page -- it's box 11 from the top of the page. Mr. Krajisnik is the speaker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: That's in B/C/S, page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's where it starts with "Jeli" [phoen]. Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please read that aloud.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: The relevant line is "Jeli Atisula" [phoen].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note this could be translated in at least three ways. One would be "has it gone" "has it been dispatched," "has it been taken care of?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And all three translations I hear the word "it" rather than "they." Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could not be "they." I see the interpreters nodding no. Mr. Tieger, that line does not refer to "they," but at least to "it," and then you have heard the three possible translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we make it clear. That was the point. So far as the three possibilities are concerned, with some slight reservation about number three, we have no big issue about that. It was the "it/they" point which has now been resolved. Thank you to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, was it common for Mr. Krajisnik to contact you about details of this nature, traffic barriers, obstacles, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. I can give you an example. At the time when the war broke out and when the roads were blocked by the warring parties, a road was being constructed near the place Trljevic [phoen] and there was heavy machinery there, to allow people to move from the lower part of Sarajevo towards Pale through the wood. So these were all everyday problems, and I informed Mr.Krajisnik when I would come down to Sarajevo.So it is possible this was the case as well, but I cannot remember what this particular conversation refers to. So over -- to Trljevic, Lukavica, and Bistrica, there was a road towards the seat of the government. There was no bypass way or the old road was impassable because it was under the control of the Muslim army, Muslim forces. They were just clearing new road through the wood. Maybe we were talking about that, but I cannot remember exactly now. But I know that Mr.Krajisnik asked me and that I informed him about everyday events that were happening there where I was, and we were quite often in contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you try make Mr. Krajisnik aware of his -- many of the details of what was happening in the area as you possibly could?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever I thought was relevant, I did inform him, as well as about whatever he asked me to tell him about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Cmeric tells me, in fact she informs me that at page 32, line 10, well, the previous line, actually, line 9, the sentence "that's when Mr. Krajisnik asked me and I reported to him about everyday events." At line 14, the witness said, "Whatever I thought was relevant I did inform him." Ms. Cmeric suggests that "informed" is the appropriate translation or interpretation at line 10, rather than "reported," or reported to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask the interpreters, first of all, whether they still remember what the witness then said, and whether "informed" would be a better translation than "report." It's not exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would kindly ask the witness to repeat his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then of course the witness is now aware of what the problem is. Then we'll -- we'll inform the interpreters at a later stage what the witness said on the basis of the audiotape rather than ask the witness now to repeat his answer. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I'd like to move to Prosecution's next in order. For the benefit of the booth, I indicated that's an intercepted conversation on Sanction. That's ET 0322-0981, and it's been previously introduced as P292 KID 31472.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. One other question, just to be very practical. The issue of report or inform, if it would be inform would that be accepted by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll certainly accept whatever the results of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, the Prosecution accepts the testimony of its witness to be informed, so that we don't have to go through the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's most helpful. Your Honour, may I just mention that in relation to the previous exhibit, the one we've just left, 443, Ms. Cmeric sent an e-mail yesterday evening to Mr. Tieger raising some points on the translation. I don't know whether Mr. Tieger has had and taken the opportunity of considering that e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear that from Mr. Tieger at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I apologise. I don't believe I was clear with the Court. I thought you were asking if any further steps would be necessary once the matter was reviewed and the interpreters made an appropriate determination of what word had been used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The first thing I asked you is if Ms. Cmeric would be right in informing, would that change the Prosecution's case in such a way that we really have to verify its -- well, it's that essential. If you say it is, then we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think I'd ask for it to be verified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll check it on the audio.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. The e-mail I mentioned had nothing to do with this point of --.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- informed. That issue, that point stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's now first continue, and whatever was in the e-mail, we'll hear about that at a later stage. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] I have the text in English. The interpreters note we don't have the English translation of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we stop. The interpreters have not the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The English booth only had the B/C/S version, but we'll get it from the B/C/S booth. Now that have the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The wrong booth had or at least one of the booths had an English translation. Could you tell us once you've received it so we can continue. Can we continue?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The booth is ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We can restart the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Miljana: Hello minister how are you. Momcilo MANDIC: All right how are you. Miljana: Just a moment, the president would like to talk to you. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Hello. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Mandic. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right. Are you a traitor as everybody else? Miljana: Minister, the connection broke up. Momcilo MANDIC: Something at your end ... Miljana: You can, laughing ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Hello. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Momo? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, President? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: What was it? Momcilo MANDIC: Probably something at your end. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: The moment I told you and you betrayed, the line got cut off. Momcilo MANDIC: God forbid. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Ah. Momcilo MANDIC: I would not do that. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Momo, tell me, how does it go. Momcilo MANDIC: Well I am not up to date with what is going on in that lower part, the main one, but as for this one, it is going well. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: These haven't come in at all ... Momcilo MANDIC: Not at all? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Not at all. Momcilo MANDIC: I would not know anything about that. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: This is a shame, a shame. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Two things. I actually wanted to see if Stanisic was there, to see with him what is happening with this, so it means that what we agreed upon was not respected. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: There is still a half chance today, and tomorrow it will be finished. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: It's a big problem with Alija. Has that one been finished? That is awful. As of today we finish it all, you know. Momcilo MANDIC: Here, there is something pounding ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Huh? Momcilo MANDIC: It could be heard that they pound. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, that is. Has he made it down there or not? It's all over now. Secondly, have you released the one I told you about by any chance? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, I have. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes? Momcilo MANDIC: He left for Vrbanja one hour ago. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Thank God. Momcilo MANDIC: Karamehmedovic, right? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, that's him. Momcilo MANDIC: Well, he is gone. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Let me also ask you what about this Savic Milos, since it's his brother, that is really ... Momcilo MANDIC: President, I put it on the list, the first next exchange and it will be finished. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Check it down there, do you have anyone there, can you contact someone? Momcilo MANDIC: There is this Vukovic, a member of the youth organisation, a Serb who is criticising us because we ... Have four hundred prisoners here, you know? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Who is criticising? Momcilo MANDIC: I've got four hundred. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And who is criticising? Momcilo MANDIC: This Vukovic, Filip, the member of youth organisation, Serb, he says clean it, but for them they are ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Filip Vukovic? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Communist? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: What does he want? Momcilo MANDIC: He is the president of that does this commission. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Their commission? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And what is that he wants? What is it that he wants? Momcilo MANDIC: War prisoners. No, they are ex for them. They are hardly interested in people. They are interested in ammunition and meat and now we let those women and children go to Vrbanja, go to -- to go to their own people. He says that ethnic cleansing what we do ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: He does. Momcilo MANDIC: ... here ... when ... I will fucking. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And where is he now. Momcilo MANDIC: Somewhere there, I do not know. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: With them, isn't he? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: That means he is theirs? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: God traitors are all around. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Good, Momo, look, please do call him. I would like to help Savic. It's his brother in stake. Momcilo MANDIC: First exchange I will take care of that. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Good, Momo. Momcilo MANDIC: And that man, is he gone? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Momo let me ask you something. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Whom should we appoint for the public prosecutor? Momcilo MANDIC: Avlijas Slobodan. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Avlijas Slobodan? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well is that ... Momcilo MANDIC: It is, President, here, there is a man who knows everybody who is from here ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I know him. Momcilo MANDIC: So, do you know him? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Good, if he was pro ... judge ... Momcilo MANDIC: He was medj [phoen] ... he was in my ministry, however, he is skilled, capable, he knows many of those people, and the place does not hold him. I think he is the man for it. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Kovac Slobodan, this one cannot. Momcilo MANDIC: Kovac Slobodan what? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Good. Momcilo MANDIC: Already ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: You should draft that proposal, and then send it from here. Momcilo MANDIC: Deal. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right. Momcilo MANDIC: Bye. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Come on, go back to work. You are hardly there yourself ... really ... listen, you say I will give the fax and you do it straight away. You say I will give the phone and you do it straight away. Momcilo MANDIC: [Laughing] Momcilo KRAJISNIK: We should set you free from this fax because ... Momcilo MANDIC: Don't ... will come ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: You don't have to ... Momcilo MANDIC: Skrbo is here. I don't know what to do with him. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Don't go to the field now, for action ... Momcilo MANDIC: Laughing ... no, no, no ... President what are we going to do, do send a commissioner to Kasindol, two three men some Papazi [phoen], they came to me from Dr. Avramovic from Kasindol, nobody ever called, they scattered there, doctor. They appoint their own people for directors. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And who is that one? Momcilo MANDIC: To Kasindol, the hospital. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Who are those people, where is that from. Momcilo MANDIC: Local community of Kasindol, the Crisis Staff. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And is that municipality, which one? Momcilo MANDIC: No it's local community Ilidza, Ilidza is the municipality Kasindol is the local community. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And why do they have the commissioner, why don't they go there. Momcilo MANDIC: No, it isn't. I don't know which ... these doctors came to me. They appointed some -- Divljan Sonja instead of this director ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And how could they do that? Momcilo MANDIC: The Crisis Staff of the local community Kasindol appointed her. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Give me please ... Momcilo MANDIC: And then -- Popovic Koviljka the cashier to make an overview to see how the income is being distributed and income again ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I will now call Prstojevic to go there or to send someone because he has the Crisis Staff Ilidza and that is Ilidza. Momcilo MANDIC: It's a shame President. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I will see that they take care of that immediately. Momcilo MANDIC: But they are in contact with Prstojevic. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: See, then, if he does not do anything we'll see to send someone else there. Momcilo MANDIC: They are in some kind of business with that Prstojevic. They do black marketing together ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: He cannot could anything on his own, he has the committee now, some wonderful people are there, you know. They are not the old ones any more. Momcilo MANDIC: But, doctor, these came and they whine and cry ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Tell them it will be taken care of properly. Momcilo MANDIC: Because they do not obey. They did not give them a slice of bread. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Who? Momcilo MANDIC: These from the local community, because ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Who does not give a peace of bread? Momcilo MANDIC: They would not allow assistance go straight to the hospital Kasindol, but only through them. Then they stop that assistance and then give them a little. It's a shame. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I will now ... Momcilo MANDIC: People should be arrested, President. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I will find Dragan Kalinic now to go there and see what needs to be done. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, please, Doctor, do call. Here I have five people sitting here, right across me, staring at me and ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Momo, what you promised I will do. Momcilo MANDIC: Good, President. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: There is no such a minister in the entire planet ... Momcilo MANDIC: Oh, come on, please ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I will ... Momcilo MANDIC: So they don't disperse the staff. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I will, Momo. Momcilo MANDIC: Thank you very much. Bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I heard as a translation when Divljan Sonja was introduced, that she was appointed as a doctor, from what I understood, where it seems both in B/C/S and in the English translation to be director. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, does the Court wish me to go on at this point or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you have several questions, we'd rather have a break first. Yes. We'll adjourn until 10 minutes past --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just hand up the -- those -- the updated version of that -- we called it a dossier. I've got lots of copies here, Your Honour, certainly enough for the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. We'll adjourn until 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Stewart, you told us before the break that if you would not have convinced us yet that you'd like to address the Chamber ex parte on whether or not you should cross-examine the witness after the Prosecution has finished its examination-in-chief, the Chamber would like to give you an opportunity to do that, which means that we would have then, for a short while, an ex parte hearing on that. That means, Madam Registrar, I must say, it's the first time that in the course of a trial we move to an ex parte hearing. So if you have any -- apart from asking the Prosecution to leave and to go into closed session, I don't think that anything else is needed. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Might I have just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of the questions is whether we can separate the transcript, because it should be a separate transcript. Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That struck me, Your Honour. And, yes, thank you for raising it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be limited in time, but Mr. Stewart said that he doesn't want to, of course, to put his strategy on the table, which is -- the Chamber thinks an understandable position, and therefore I'd like to go into closed session and to ask the Prosecution to leave the courtroom, and ask transcribers and technicians whether this would be sufficient to have a separate transcript. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have a correction, just one - probably there would be many others - from the last transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The interpreters -- before we go into closed session, the interpreters have one correction for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In the last transcript, wherever it says "it's a shame," the right way of translating it would be "it's a disgrace." And both speakers used the word. The French booth translated it properly. They said, "c'est une honte."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and the only thing I could say, that if only such small mistakes were made where you have such an enormous task, then everyone would admire the job the interpreters are doing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We were again reading from the transcript given. We were not interpreting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm identified that the technicians would need ten minutes after the ex parte hearing, and since the Chamber might need some time to make up its mind on the decision. We'll then now turn into a closed and ex parte hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 4.20 p.m., to be followed by an Ex Parte hearing

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we started a new transcript. Therefore, Madam Registrar, could I ask you to call the case. Is it just a new transcript and not -- okay. Then that's not needed, although of course we are sitting and hearing the case of the Prosecution against Mr. Krajisnik. First of all, before we continue, I should explain to both parties what technical problems we faced. As a matter of fact, an ex parte hearing means that, of course, the other party should not be aware of what has been said. Since we continued, the ex parte hearing would have been available to the OTP on their laptop computers. Therefore, I instructed, and I should have foreseen this, and I should have warned you in advance, I instructed the technicians to remove the part prior to the break from your laptop computers. You'll get the open session back as soon as possible, but it is in order to get rid of the ex parte part. Therefore, I had to do that, and I apologise for not having foreseen better the technical problems an ex parte hearing just in the middle of a trial would take. Having explained this, if it would cause you any problem, I still might have my -- so if there's any need to consult the transcript of the open session, then we could do that. And this was all to hear the Defence on the issue on whether or not the Defence is expected to cross-examine Mr. Mandic. The decision of the Chamber does not only deal with the matter of cross-examination of Mr. Mandic, but is split up in four parts. First part: In view of the very special circumstances that have arisen now, the Prosecution is ordered to provide the Article 68 material that had been disclosed, I think it was yesterday, to the Defence, not only in B/C/S but also in translation, so that counsel can have access to it. And when I say in one of the official languages of the Tribunal, that, of course, means in English under those circumstances. Second: The Prosecution should not touch upon this material during its examination-in-chief. And if the Prosecution would touch upon any material that was for the first time disclosed to the Defence after the 29th of October, it should indicate so, so that the Chamber can then decide whether or not it will allow the introduction of that material into evidence or at least directly related to the testimony of the witness. If, in accordance with this guidance, the Prosecution refrains from touching upon that material, that Article 68 material recently disclosed, and if it follows the instruction to inform the Chamber as soon as any material is touched upon directly, which was for the first time disclosed after the 29th of October, 2004, if the OTP keeps to that instruction, then the Defence is given the opportunity to cross-examine Mr. Mandic once the OTP has finished its examination-in-chief. The Defence is further entitled to apply, if need be, ex parte, if that would be needed in order to establish good cause and not to damage the interests of the Defence, the Defence is entitled to apply for further cross-examination of Mr. Mandic if material that was disclosed for the first time after the 29th of October would cause them to do so. This is the ruling of the Chamber on these matters. Then, Mr. Tieger, are you ready to resume the cross-examination of the witness? I'm now confused. It's late Friday evening, Friday afternoon. Is it clear to you, or do you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe it's clear, Your Honour. However, I think I'm going to need to retrieve some materials in order to comply fully with the Court's -- I don't have the disclosure history in front of me and would not necessarily be able to identify those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I saw that the disclosure history at least was on the list of Mr. Stewart. Item 2 says final exhibit list and disclosure history, which is 6.290 kilobytes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. We may have to move a little bit slower, but we'll certainly endeavour to do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Madam Usher, unless there are any questions the Defence would like to ask in relation to this ruling. Perhaps one clarification. Where I said that the Chamber gives an opportunity to the Defence to cross-examine the witness, of course I cannot instruct the Defence to cross-examine the witness because it's finally up to the Defence whether or not to cross-examine the witness. That's why I used the words that the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We appreciated the terms in which Your Honour clearly carefully and, with respect, correctly chosen the phraseology. May I just consult my colleagues for one moment. I think there may be just one point, Your Honour, where we might ask for some clarification. Excuse me one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, one moment, Your Honour. I'm going to have to scroll back a little bit on the ... Your Honour, the only question we raise is Your Honour mentioned - I hope I'm near enough to the microphone - Your Honour said, and this is at page -- which page are we on here? Page 2. Page 2, oh, because it's a new transcript. Page 2, line 7, the second point in your -- the Trial Chamber's ruling. "The Prosecution should not touch upon this material during its examination-in-chief. And if the Prosecution would touch upon any material that was for the first time disclosed to the Defence after the 29th of October, it should indicate so, so that the Chamber can then decide whether or not it will allow the introduction of that material into evidence or at least directly related to the testimony of the witness." And Your Honour, the question we ask is, and this would need to be checked, but we think the position may be that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It had been done already.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Material introduced into evidence was introduced after the 29th of October. So it would seem logically that that part of the ruling ought in some way apply to that. In which case I suppose my question is, I'm sorry to put it so lamely, but where does that leave us, Your Honour, with respect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, we'll what then do is -- of course, the Prosecution could not take into consideration any decision not yet taken by the Trial Chamber. So therefore, we'll then see where our attention should then be drawn now by the Prosecution to that material already introduced, and we'll then have to decide whether that still is in evidence, whether that's -- or whether an extra opportunity would be given to the Defence to have a delayed cross-examination. We'll then decide on the basis of what we find. Of course, it very much also depends on what material that is. So, therefore, if such material has already been introduced into evidence, material that had never been disclosed before the 29th of October, then the Chamber would like to be informed. Because we have two categories now. We have the late Article 68 disclosure, which is out -- well, it's not out, but if it's touched upon directly by the Prosecution, then the condition under which the Chamber will ask the Defence to cross-examine the witness is not fulfilled any more, and then, so therefore, that part, the third part of the ruling then does not stand. We have another category of material that is -- apart from this Article 68 material, any material disclosed after the 29th of October for the first time. And if that has been introduced already, the Chamber would like to be informed to consider whether this needs any further decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. There's just one practical question, Your Honour. Clearly, a first step for all concerned on the counsel's side is to try and be clear what material has been disclosed for the first time since the 29th of October. But I'm sure we're all interested in avoiding duplication of effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that -- I take it that perhaps the first -- I mean part of the problem is related - if it's new material - by late disclosure. So therefore, I would like to invite the Prosecution to give its view on any material used in court after -- and disclosed for the first time after the 29th of October, to give -- to at least to inform the Defence what documents would meet that criterion, and then of course if the parties will disagree, we'll hear that later. I take it the examination-in-chief will not be finished today anyhow, so even if that would be done over the weekend, then we'll be confronted with it on Monday, and whenever needed, we'll give any further rulings. Yes? Is that clear? If that's clear, then I'd like to ask Madam Usher to escort the witness and Mr. Tomic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, since you're a trained lawyer, you'll certainly understand that procedural issues sometimes take more time than one would wish. But we're now back to the substance. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, before we recessed, we were looking at a telephone conversation of June 26th, 1992, between you and Mr. Krajisnik. I take it you still have the transcript of that conversation before you. You seem to be looking at the transcript. I gather it's there in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in that conversation, you refer to having 400 prisoners here. Do you see that part of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, did you ever try to hide or keep from Mr. Krajisnik information about the number of prisoners who were detained on Bosnian Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, these are not prisoners. These are people who were removed from the war area where there was fighting. I informed Mr. Krajisnik when I was down there that I immediately removed these people from that territory, and I sent them via Vrbanja Most to Sarajevo. Actually, I think that at that time there was fighting around the airport and the neighbourhood of Dobrinja, which is very close to Kula. That was my initiative. Without commissions, without lists, that these people be removed from the area where there was fighting. I informed Krajisnik about that, and Mr. Krajisnik asked me about Mr. Karamehmedovic, to find him and ensure his safe return to Sarajevo. That's what I did. I did return him and I informed him about that. Can I tell you about one more thing? This Vukovic, who was chairman of the commission of the Federation, he did not want to receive these people, because he probably had a problem with food and accommodation. So they created a problem over this, saying that it was ethnic cleansing. If there is population living in a war-torn area, and if you ask them where they want to go, and if they say "we want to go to Sarajevo to stay with our relatives, friends," whatever, that's exactly what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me -- may I ask that Exhibit P439 be presented to the witness once again. Meanwhile, he can keep the transcript of this conversation. Mr. Mandic, I want to direct your attention to the last full paragraph of that document, the one that appears to begin immediately after the names toward the bottom of page 2 of the B/C/S version of Nijaz Sukric and Ibrahim Dzenanovic. Do you see where that paragraph begins?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to refresh everyone's recollection, P439 is a document that was sent by Mr. Vukovic, the gentleman mentioned in the telephone conversation of June 26th. Now, at that portion of the document that I directed you to, Mr. Vukovic states: "We believe that once your side has fulfilled the previously arranged exchanges, we should embark on the release of all imprisoned persons and detainees, in accordance with the agreement reached at UNPROFOR on 9 June 1992. The attachment contains the list of imprisoned persons and detainees according to our records. It is our opinion that, once released, the detainees should be sent to their places of residence, i.e., to their domicile address. Otherwise, this would signify typical deportation, exile, and ethnic cleansing of the area. Such persons should also be issued with appropriate certificates to prevent arrests for the second or third time." And as we discussed yesterday -- well, let me first ask you: Is this the allegation by Mr. Vukovic to which you were referring in your conversation with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I can't remember. I believe it is, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And again, looking at P439, the list of imprisoned persons and detainees that Mr. Vukovic was referring to was the list he provided in an attachment to the same document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me go back a moment to the question I asked you before. Here in this conversation, you're informing Mr. Krajisnik about 400 people who are held by the Bosnian Serb authorities. Did you ever keep from him or hide from him information about persons who were being held by Bosnian Serb authorities that was in your -- that you knew about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At my own discretion, I informed Mr. Krajisnik about these people who, at my own initiative and with the consent of Minister Stanisic and the chief of police, Tepavcevic, who then held Kula, Milo Tepavcevic, nicknamed Tepo. I asked for assistance and I let these people go to Sarajevo, which was under Muslim control. Because these people were at that moment in a territory where fighting was still raging, police fighting, I think around the airport. Because this was a separation between Ilidza, that was held by the Serb forces, and the other part, the eastern part, that was also held by the Serb forces. So in passing, I informed him about this, and Krajisnik had called me because of Mr. Savic and Mr. Karamehmedovic and that's why he sent me to Sarajevo, to find him, and to hand him over at Vrbanja Most to his family, and it was probably something that someone had asked Mr. Krajisnik to do, an acquaintance or somebody. And when I spoke about those obstacles or whatever before, it was 20 kilometres, say, from Pale, or from the Hotel Bistrica, where the government was, down to Lukavica. And this communication was impeded. The road was not an easy one. It was a forest road. And, in passing, I informed him about these problems at the local commune, the doctor, the food, and everything else that was going on there, and that I thought I should inform him about. Mr. Prosecutor, I believe that this list does not refer to this transcript. This list was probably given to Ratko, because at that time there was no chairman of the commission. I think that Vanovac was appointed. So there was this administration and there was a bit of confusion there because the Serb side did not have a very high degree of organisation. I helped ad hoc, or if Krajisnik or anybody else asked me to do them a favour in terms of the people who were being kept, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you inform Mr. Krajisnik about the list of 3.441 prisoners identified in the attachment provided by Mr. Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I never saw this list or this document, never. That is what I assert before this honourable Trial Chamber. I never saw this in all my life, this list or this document, nor did I ever work on this list. That is what I assert under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On June 26th, 1992, Mr. Vukovic faxed this document -- this document was faxed --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness's answer to that last question: "I never saw this list or document, never." We believe that that is precisely what the witness said yesterday, in which case, the question that was asked: "Did you inform Mr. Krajisnik about the list of 3.441 prisoners identified in the attachment provided by Mr. Vukovic?" It's -- well, we suppose that it's an inadvertent question based on overlooking the fact that he had previously said that he had never seen it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Tieger, you take that point. If you say I haven't seen the list, then it's difficult to say I -- or would you consider it a coincidence that 3.441 people would be exactly the same on the basis of ... Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think -- I have found and I have expressed the view that Mr. Stewart, a very alert counsel, has a custom of intervening in an examination before a particular area has been concluded. That's what's happening now. I'd like to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree with Mr. Stewart that your question suggests something the witness denied to be the fact, and so therefore, in one way or the other, it should be made explicit then on what basis the question is put to the witness. Once the witness had answered this question, Mr. Stewart, there was no need for further intervention, I think, unless you'd say that the next question was about that same list. But, therefore, I try to do it shortly, Mr. Tieger, to better -- you took the point that any direct reference in relation to this witness to that list might not be the best thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, of I was mainly concerned to ensure that it was done inadvertently, because I must remind the Trial Chamber, this is Mr. Tieger's witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's continue. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger, and I urge the parties not to intervene unnecessarily, certainly not unnecessarily. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On the 26th of June, P439, the document by Mr. Vukovic was faxed -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you. I'll repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On June 26th, 1992, P439, the document that we've been referring to by Mr. Vukovic, was faxed to the Central Commission for the Exchange of Persons. And on that same date, you had your conversation with Mr. Krajisnik, during which you made reference to Mr. Vukovic's allegations about ethnic cleansing. How did you learn about Mr. Vukovic's claims that ethnic cleansing, or concern that ethnic cleansing was taking place?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably one of my co-workers told me, people who were in contact with Vukovic, or maybe when I was in personal contact with him. I cannot remember how this happened. You see, when I got there to those premises, and when I saw a great many people in one place, and when I asked them where are you from, what are you doing here, they said they were from Dobrinja and these neighbourhoods near the places where the actual fighting was going on. I asked Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Tepavcevic to give these people escorts. I asked them: Where do you want to go? And they said: We want to go and join our own people. We want to cross Vrbanja Most and go to Sarajevo. I provided them with an escort. I did that this as a humanist, as a former Sarajevo policeman. I knew half of these people. I made it possible for them to get to Vrbanja Most and it's by chance that I informed Krajisnik about that, because I was doing other things that day, telling him about the problems with the doctors, and the fact that I found this Karamehmedovic, that Mr. Krajisnik asked to transfer to Sarajevo. At one point in time Krajisnik says thank God that he got to Vrbanja Most alive, because he probably promised this man from Sarajevo, or rather, these people from Sarajevo who were relatives of Karamehmedovic that we would find the man and take him back to his family. But I didn't manage to take care of this other problem. This person who worked with Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Savic. The problem he had with his brother. Although I was supposed to do that at the request and at the behest of the president of the parliament. That's what I did, from those positions. I'm not going into these lists. It was lower-ranking officials to dealt with this, Mr. Prosecutor. It says Ratko here. Perhaps this was sent to Ratko Lalovic, who was already warden of the prison, who was already working there. It was not the job of the minister. There was a central commission. Now whether it's the Sarajevo Central Commission, or the state Central Commission, you cannot see that from here. I am really not familiar with these lists and these commissions and I really can't help you on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I might have missed it, but where did you see these 400 people who were being held? Where were they being held?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, at that time, I was building the Serb judiciary. At the location of Kula, where there was a semi-open prison before the war, and an investigation prison. There were a few buildings there and that is where I set up the district court of the Serb Sarajevo, the basic court of the Serb Sarajevo, the basic prosecutor's office, the higher prosecutor's office, and I asked for the police and army to leave the Kula prison so that it could become a part of the district court in Sarajevo as an investigation office. At that time, I spent a lot of time there, because I was looking for Serbs who were eminent lawyers, who were leaving the federal town of Sarajevo, like Milan Trbojevic, Marko Arsovic, Sveto Stanojevic, and many, many others. That's where I kept them. And then we were building a judiciary at that locality. When I passed there, I saw a large number of people there. I saw war operations. And then I got involved as a person who wanted to solve a problem, because this was still the beginning of the war. And there were operations going on and people were wondering what to do. They didn't know who had what kind of authority. So at my own initiative, I transferred these people, with the assistance of the MUP, who held Kula then, and they safely reached Vrbanja Most and crossed it. That's what I did, Mr. Prosecutor. And then on the 20th of May, that's the day when I became minister, I went down and all the people who were there at that moment, I safely transferred them to Vrbanja Most. And you have Mr. Tepavcevic's note about that, but the other one. He was chief of police there at Kula and he held the police station there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Why did you advise Mr. Krajisnik about the 400 prisoners and what Mr. Vukovic had said about them? Was it because you wanted him to know that there were 400 people being held or because you wanted him to know about Mr. Vukovic's concerns or allegations, or for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeated this to you yesterday, and I'm repeating it again today. For the most part, I informed Mr. Krajisnik because I trusted him the most when compared to all the Serb leaders. So I thought what I should tell him -- I mean, I'm from Sarajevo. I lived in Sarajevo for 40 years. And Mr. Krajisnik was born in Sarajevo too. And then I thought that perhaps Karadzic or Mladic would not be too worried about that kind of thing. I thought that he was the person that I should tell about this situation in the lower Sarajevo, Donja Sarajevo, down there. And I spent a lot of time down there as I was building the judiciary. I did this at my own initiative, because the basic purpose of our conversation was who the republican prosecutor should be and whether Savic's brother was exchanged and whether everything was all right with Mr. Karamehmedovic. Is that the right name? Yes. The previous day, he asked me, requested me, or rather, told me simply to find the man and to return him to Sarajevo, to his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Krajisnik ask you why Vukovic was saying that what the Bosnian Serbs were doing was ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, please. As far as I can remember -- as for Mr. Vukovic's position, the one that's written down here, it's either Ratko Lalovic or somebody else who informed me about this. I don't know exactly who it was. And then I conveyed his position and his opinion to Mr. Krajisnik. Or perhaps Mr. Vukovic told me when I was looking for Mr. Savic's family. I cannot tell you exactly. This was 12 years ago, how I learned about this position of his. But I saw those people there, terrified, with these bundles, women, children. When I asked them: Where do you want to go? And they said: We want to go to Sarajevo. We want to go via Vrbanja Most. I think that the only thing that crossed my mind at that moment was to get those people and those children out of the war zone, or rather, the area surrounding Kula. So it's from that position that I did that, Mr. Prosecutor. Krajisnik did not know about this. Had I not told him about it, he wouldn't have known about it. All this information concerning things that were going on there, he received from me, because I was, yes, one of the people who enjoyed his confidence, one of the people that he trusted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you know that there were others -- did you know whether there were others, other Muslims, being held by the Bosnian Serbs at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Kula, the Kula prison?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Kula or anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The establishment of the ministry -- or in mid-May I became minister. One of the priority tasks was to create a judiciary, and the next step was, in accordance with the decision made by the government, I think, to dissolve all municipal camps, or rather, these places where civilians were held in the territory of the entire Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that moment, when I came to Kula, it is correct, Mr. Prosecutor, that I did see people who were not of Serb ethnicity, that I saw them in Kula, and every time Mr. Tepavcevic told either me or Mr. Stanisic or the Central Commission about the war operations and whether it was the army or the police that had jurisdiction over them. You have two or three letters from Mr. Tepavcevic in which he informs the minister of police, or rather, the chief of the public security, the minister of the judiciary, and other institutions, about the situation in Kula that was then held by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So it -- in addition to the 400 people who were the subject of discussion in the June 26th conversation, did you know at that time that there were others, other non-Serbs who were being held in various places around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that somewhere in Lukavica, the army also had a centre where imprisoned non-Serbs were held. This is in Lukavica, but that was exclusively under the jurisdiction of the army. There is something that corroborates what I've been claiming all along. When Mr. Krajisnik was asking me about Karamehmedovic, I said I'll see whether he's in Lukavica or in Kula. Lukavica was held by the military, and that's about three kilometres away from Kula. It was the Sarajevo Corps, the military, that held Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When Mr. Colovic or Mr. Tepavcevic or whoever it was that informed you about Mr. Vukovic's document tell -- or told you about Mr. Vukovic's allegations, did he also tell you about the 3.441 persons on the list?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you for the third time, Mr. Prosecutor: Never in my life did I see or hear about this list of 3.000-something people. I never saw any such thing. Either Mr. Vukovic, from that commission, or somebody else from the administration, told me about Mr. Vukovic's position, that people in that area should not return to Sarajevo but, rather, that they should stay there. And that was considered to be ethnic cleansing. If from Dobrinja they go to Marin Dvor. Dobrinja was engulfed by war operations. There was fighting there. And in Marin Dvor there was nothing. So from that point of view he said it was ethnic cleansing. I thought it was better to transfer them there so that something would not happen to someone. Call it ethnic cleansing if you will. But there were women, children there, in prison, without proper hygienic conditions, nothing. It was an enormous number of people for this small prison that was only an investigation, semi-open prison before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Given your position as minister of justice and the work you were doing for -- in connection with exchanges at that time, as we discussed yesterday, would you have expected anyone who received the document from Mr. Vukovic to tell you about that list of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By looking at this fax number, you can establish whose number that is, whether that was the police station, or rather, the SUP in Kula, or the office of somebody else. It says here Ratko. That means that Ratko was the person who received this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, may I just stop you. Would you please carefully listen to the question. The question was not to whom this list was sent. The question was whether you, in your position, as minister of justice, whether you would have expected anyone who received the document, whoever that was, to tell you about that list. That's the question. Would you please focus your answer on that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. Prosecutor. Can you please repeat the question. I was a little bit confused by this intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, we've spoken about a list of almost three and a half thousand prisoners, a list you wouldn't know. The question, quite simply, is that if someone would have received that list, whether you would expect, as minister of justice, to be informed about such a number of imprisoned persons or persons detained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you eventually find out about the presence of that number of persons in Bosnian Serb territory or about efforts by the Commission for Exchange -- by the Bosnian Commission for Exchange to obtain their release?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that seems to be two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the witness, I think, could split them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, the witness may answer the question. The questions are sometimes a bit complicated. If the witness doesn't understand the question, if he doesn't see the two elements in it, he'll tell us. So the question was whether you finally found out about the presence of such a number of persons on your territory, and Mr. Tieger was referring to detained or imprisoned persons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you referring to the entire territory of Republika Srpska or just the area around -- in and around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's begin with the area in and around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never familiar with the list of imprisoned people. That was exclusively under the responsibility of municipal and Central Commissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, may I stop you. The question was not about the list as such, but about such a number of people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know how many imprisoned people were in the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was: The area of Sarajevo, whether you became aware of a number of approximately, well, let's say, three and a half thousand people imprisoned or detained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed with the second part of your question. Perhaps I can put it to you. Did you ever find out that, well, let's say the other side was trying to get a release of those persons or of such a number of persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you referring to the other warring party, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, how to reconcile your answer that you never found out about such a number present in that area, although you say that you -- the other party was seeking to have them released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were in contact constantly with the State Commission of Republika Srpska and the Federal State Commission for Exchange, and I know the people insisted on these exchanges to be carried out by both sides, without mentioning any numbers. I never knew how many people were detained at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you are not even aware that these were numbers, well, close to at least a few thousand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never heard the exact numbers, and I was never informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking about the exact numbers. I'm asking about approximate numbers, whether it be two thousand, three thousand, 2.500.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you, as minister of justice, you were interested to know, or were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since there was the State Commission, and people from all government levels were involved in that, that was their responsibility; and, on the other hand, I was very often in Sarajevo and other towns, where I was trying to build the judiciary structure. They did inform me whether there were or were not people, but about numbers and exchanges, I was never interested in that, because I believe that not to be part of my jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You had no idea whether this exchange was about ten people or a hundred people or a thousand people? You had no idea about the approximate size of the number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were several commissions, Your Honour. In Grbavica, there was a man, I think Bulajic he was responsible on behalf of the commission for exchanges. There was Vanovac, who was also responsible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'm not asking who was responsible for the exchange. My question was whether you had an approximate -- an idea of the approximate number of people involved in these exchanges. And I asked you whether you knew whether it was ten, a hundred, a thousand, a few thousand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You had no idea.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew nothing about numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Would you refrain from seeking contact, then, Mr. Tomic. May I instruct you not to express in whatever way anything in the direction of the witness. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, during the conversation of June 26 with Mr. Krajisnik, as you've indicated, he sought the -- or inquired about Mr. Karamehmedovic and whether or not he'd been released, and I believe you indicated yesterday that on other occasions, Mr. Krajisnik had sought the release of friends. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, were these friends whose release was sought by Mr. Krajisnik people who had engaged in combat or taken up arms against the Bosnian Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
