utterances.text: I knew nothing about that, and I never inquired who these people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were they people, as far as you knew, who were suspected of any crimes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know how subordination and superiority in the government functions. If somebody told me: Mandic, go there, and Karamehmedovic was either in Kula or in Lukavica, where the army was running the centre, it is important for me to have this man return to Sarajevo. I carried out this order, I acted as a soldier carrying out his order. If I found the man there, I would ask the army to release him, or if -- or the police who were holding them, I would tell them that Mr. Krajisnik had ordered me to bring this man to Vrbanja and that he be released to go back to Sarajevo. And I would personally escort this person and then inform Mr. Krajisnik that I had carried out his instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Court may wish to go on. I'm only pausing because I don't know whether given the stops and starts whether the Court wishes to stick with the normal schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm afraid we can't stick with the normal schedule to the extent that we might be running out of tapes. I would say if -- have you dealt with this document or would you continue with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think I'm finished with the document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Tieger, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'll repeat what you said. You think you're finished with the document. We'll have a break, but before having a break, I'd like to ask a few questions to the witness in relation to this document first. Mr. Mandic, I'm interested in that 400 people that were in Kula, as you told us. Were they men, women, children? What was the composition? More or less, not in detail, of course, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there were men, women, and children, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ages? All ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was a long time ago. It's difficult for me to remember. But I do know that they had come from the Dobrinja neighbourhood, that they had been frightened, and that they wanted to leave that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were they exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. On my own initiative, and with the approval of Mico Stanisic and Tepavcevic, who were heads of the police, took those people to the Vrbanja Most, which is a borderline between the Serbian-controlled Sarajevo and the federal Sarajevo, and I escorted them wherever they wanted to go. I did that without any knowledge of any Exchange Commission or whoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that would be true for the men in the group as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the people who were in this group I took across the Vrbanja Most to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to that part of the transcript of the intercept, where it reads -- it's in English. It's the third page, but I'll read it in its entirety to you so that you can hear it. When Mr. Krajisnik asked: "And what is that he wants?", referring to Mr. Vukovic. You said: "War prisoners. No, they're ex for them. They're hardly interested in people. They're interested in ammunition and meat, and now we let those women and children go to Vrbanja, to go to their own people. He says that's ethnic cleansing what we do." You make reference to women and children to be brought to Vrbanja. Could you explain this part of your conversation, where you said they were not interested in -- they were interested in -- or they were not interested in people, and you mentioned war prisoners in that respect. Could you explain this part, and also why you only referred to women and children when you said that you let those go to Vrbanja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I took that group to Vrbanja, the problem was that the Sarajevo authorities didn't want to receive them. They had problems with the food. And, for instance -- this may be switching to another subject, perhaps. At the time, the Sarajevo authorities didn't even allow children to leave Sarajevo. The problem they had was food and accommodation. That's at least how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did these 400 people have a place to go, a house, whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked them where they wanted to go, and they told me that they wanted to go to Sarajevo, where their government and their authority was, where their relatives were. And once they told me that that was their wish, I brought them to this borderline. They just wanted to leave the Kula area, where I had found them. And I fulfilled their request at my own initiative and I transferred these people to safety. Whether they had accommodation provided them or not, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did any of them ask you to stay in the, well, Serb-controlled territory and, for example, go to family there or to ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this particular case, I don't remember. I think that they all wanted to leave, because there was shooting and fighting around the airport. The Dobrinja neighbourhood was very close to Kula, and they wanted to escape from the area where there were war operations. No one wanted to stay behind. Later, or even before that, it did happen that people wanted to go either to Serbia or Montenegro just to escape the war-torn zones, and then those people were transported by buses to Pale, first if they had family members in Serbia or Montenegro, they were handed over to the Red Cross, and that was undertaken by the Ministry of Health. I think that the minister at the time was Dragan Kalinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say: "I think that they all wanted to leave because there was shooting or fighting." How did you verify that? Not the shooting and the fighting, but the wish to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went inside. I asked them where they were from. Some of them knew me personally, because before the war I was living all the time in Sarajevo. I was a well-known sportsman. And they asked me: Please help us leave this area. We have families in Sarajevo. And the whole group who were frightened couldn't wait for us to provide escort for them to take them to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, at any later group, was there any exchange of later groups? Because you said these 400 at that time, and then later the exchange ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was never -- I never carried out exchanges. However, very often, at the request of my friends or acquaintances from Sarajevo, went to either of the prisons where I found people or family members, relatives of my acquaintances and friends, and took them to where they wanted to go. I can give you the examples. I can give you the names of those people, if it is relevant for this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These were my questions for the time being. We'll have a break until 20 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness and Mr. Tomic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to Prosecution's next in order. That's another intercepted telephone conversation bearing the ERN ET 0322-0195, for the benefit of the booth, that's also on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it on an existing CD, Mr. Tieger, or is it ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll be delivering the CD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. The CD will then get number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P443, and the transcript, P443.A.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'll indicate, Your Honour, as we're about to begin, that this is a conversation between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Mandic on July 1st, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Unidentified female: Hello? Sipcic: Good afternoon, gorgeous. Unidentified female: Good afternoon. Sipcic: Sipcic. Unidentified female: Excuse me? Sipcic: Colonel Sipcic. Unidentified female: Hey, good afternoon. How are you? Sipcic: I'm okay. Thank you. Unidentified female: Um ... I'm not used to this form of address, you know ... Sipcic: Tell me, is your boss in? Unidentified female: Yes, the minister is in. Please hold on, Colonel. Sipcic: Please ... Momcilo MANDIC: Hello? Sipcic: Hello, Mr. Minister. Momcilo MANDIC: Hello, General. Sipcic: Where the heck have you been? Momcilo MANDIC: I'm right here. Yesterday I ... You weren't working. You weren't there? Sipcic: What do you mean I wasn't? Yesterday was the worst day of my life. Momcilo MANDIC: Either yesterday or the day before. It must have been yesterday you weren't there. Your fellow countryman would have known ... Sipcic: ... Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, yes, it was around 1200 hours. Sipcic: I was in the field. Will you stop by? Momcilo MANDIC: I will. Sipcic: Here, the president wants to talk to you. Hello? Momcilo MANDIC: Sure. I'll come by. When will you be free? Sipcic: I'll be here all the time. Momcilo MANDIC: All right. I'll come when they're done. Sipcic: All right. Momcilo MANDIC: Deal. Sipcic: Hold on. Momcilo MANDIC: I'll see you. Momcilo MANDIC: Hello. Radovan KARADZIC: All the best, Mr. President. Radovan KARADZIC: What's up, Momo. Momcilo MANDIC: Well not much. I've just been to a government session and I'm here now. Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. Momcilo MANDIC: We're working on an exchange now. We're evacuating some Serbs from Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija. Radovan KARADZIC: Oh, that's very important. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: We'll immediately /mobilise/ those fit for combat and the rest of them ... Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, yes, we're evacuating them. Radovan KARADZIC: How many will there be? Momcilo MANDIC: Well, I don't really know. We have many on the list. There are 300 people from Hadzici, Muslims, who have been kept here for seven days. No one's inquired about them, no one seems to care. I don't know what to do. Radovan KARADZIC: Why don't ... Momcilo MANDIC: No one's interested in them, these Muslims ... Radovan KARADZIC: Yeah. Momcilo MANDIC: So we'll try to exchange them for these, um, people from Hrasnica and ... Radovan KARADZIC: Have you found that Croat in Kula for me? Momcilo MANDIC: He's not there. Radovan KARADZIC: Tomic. He must be in Kula. Momcilo MANDIC: President, he's definitely not there. All the Croats are gone. There are no more Croats in Kula. Radovan KARADZIC: No, no he was arrested earlier. He's not in Dobrinja. Momcilo MANDIC: President all Croats have been exchanged. Here, let me check again and I'll call you back in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, should we take out the two pages which seem -- St. -- Archangel Michael, Patron Saint's Day, the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I noticed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everyone is invited to take out what seems to be a press clipping rather than a transcript of an intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me. Is this 411 and 443 or one of them? We're just trying to keep track of exhibits here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It wasn't 411 as well, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please check what's 411, because there seems to be some confusion. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll check meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I agree. We can straighten out the exhibit number. I appreciate that. We'll certainly be looking for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, Exhibit 443, as we indicated, is a conversation between you and Dr. Karadzic on July 1st, 1992. As you can see from the -- as you may have noticed from the transcript, the portion which was played in Court is not the entirety of the recorded conversation that took place. As you can see from the bottom of your transcript, it ends where you say: "I'll be there in a half-hour or so and I'll call you back in five or ten minutes." Dr. Karadzic says: "Deal." And you say: "Have a good one. See you." So at some point we may be referring to some portion of the -- I'm going to try to limit my questions to that portion of the transcript that was actually played out loud, although I note that it ended where you say: "Here, let me check again and I'll call you back in five minutes." And the conversation regarding that general topic seems to continue with

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC SAYING
utterances.text: "All right. If he's not there, let's then look for him somewhere else." And you say: "Well, does the person who is asking about Tomic know where he was taken to, where he was picked up?" And

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC SAYS
utterances.text: "There were three brothers. Two of them were released in Ilidza and the third one was kept in Ilidza and transferred to Kula. That's what happened. They were arrested in Ilidza." And you say: "President, I'll call you back in five minutes." And then it seems to move to another topic. If I can direct your attention to roughly the beginning of your conversation with Dr. Karadzic after you've spoken with Sipcic. You advise him that: "We're working on an exchange now. We're evacuating some Serbs from Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija." And Dr. Karadzic says, "Oh, that's very important." You say, "Yes." And he says, "We'll immediately," and then there's the word "mobilise" in brackets, "those fit for combat and the rest of them." Can you tell us what Dr. Karadzic was indicating would be -- would happen with respect to those Serbs who were being evacuated from Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija once that evacuation was successful.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the Serbs who were not fit for fighting?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. With the Serbs who were.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would probably be handed over to the army and be mobilised for the able-bodied Serb males.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, so those Serbs from Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija were going to be brought to the --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would be handed over to the army to be mobilised and to become members of the Army of Republika Srpska. That is how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic wanted to know how many there would be, and you indicated that you weren't sure. And then you advised him that there were 300 people from Hadzici, Muslims, who had been kept here for seven days." Where were those 300 people, those 300 Muslims, being kept?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kula, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And those people, were they men, women, children, a combination?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, believe me. Most probably, since those were 300 people, or men, they could have been men, adult men. When they say "people," they may have referred to adult men, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the Serbs from Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija were going to come to the Bosnian Serb side, and those 300 people in Kula were going to go to the Muslim side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My parents used to live in Hrasnica, and in those days, I tried to pull them out from Hrasnica that was under the Muslim control, and I did that on my own initiative, and together with them, I included my neighbours, because there were very few Serbs living there. The problem was, and I told you that before we took a break, that the State Commission of the Federation and the people from Sarajevo didn't want to accept the people from Kula, for instance, these women and children from Hadzici, because there were war operations going on. They probably had problems with accommodation, food, et cetera. I asked Mr. Tepavcevic and Ratko and these administration clerks not to have these people stay there, but rather to have them leave the area. I came to the conclusion that people were waiting there for seven days, that nobody wanted to take them in and nobody was expressing any interest in them. That's the problem that I presented to Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you explain to Dr. Karadzic who those people were and how they had come to be at Kula?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably -- well, no. No, I didn't. You can see from the telephone conversation itself that I didn't explain. Most probably, these were people from Hadzici who the police from Hadzici brought to Kula. Because the Serb forces held the municipality of Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You indicated that you didn't explain to Dr. Karadzic who those people in Kula were. Was it your understanding at the time the conversation took place that he didn't require an explanation of who they were because he already knew about them?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Sipcic was at the Slavisa Vajner Cica barracks. That's the name before the war. That's 200 miles away from Kula. So I was coming from the government session that was held probably at the Bistrica hotel in Jahorina, and when I came, I explained to them that I had just arrived five minutes before that and that I had received information that there were these people here who had been there for seven days already, either Tepavcevic or somebody else had told me about that. So I informed the president of Republika Srpska what this was all about. He did not express particular interest in this, but I believe that he knew what this was all about, because police and military structures informed him about what was going on in the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By the way, you mentioned your efforts to get your parents out of Hrasnica. Did your parents want to leave Hrasnica or did they want to stay, as it turned out?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to go into that, if at all possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't think that's such an important issue at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I seek to clarify an earlier answer of the witness, Mr. Tieger. But I'll first give you, Mr. Mandic, the time you need. If you need more time, tell me. If you are ready to respond to my next questions, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mandic, you explained to us about the 300 people from Hadzici, and you explained that no one wanted to receive them. You said they were waiting for seven days. Earlier you were asked whether these were men or -- and then you said: I don't remember. But that might have been a reference to men, the word "people" used. Here you say in your last answer, you say "women and children." "These women and children from Hadzici." Does that mean that you now do remember that these were women and children? You said the people from Sarajevo didn't want to accept the people from Kula. For instance, "these women and children from Hadzici, because there were war operations going on." And then later on you referred to the seven days they had been waiting. Were there women and children included?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said no one was interested to receive them, and you explained that by saying that: "They probably had problems with accommodation, food, et cetera." Now, they were not interested, as you told us, to receive these women and children. A few lines later, you say: "So we'll try to exchange them for these, um, people from Hrasnica." If no one is interested to receive them, would they be encouraged by your request to get people from Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I often went down there to Kula, and I insisted -- I asked Mr. Tepavcevic and these other people not to keep these persons who were put there due to war operations in the prison, to get them out of there as soon as possible, either to Sarajevo or elsewhere, or if somebody wanted to go to Serbia, Montenegro, or some other area. But there were children there and women there and adult men, that they should not be kept there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. That's what I understand. But now, from this telephone conversation, I understand that you'd like to have Serbs from Hrasnica to, as far as I understand, to immediately mobilise those fit for combat. So I take it these were men of military age, or at least, well, unless you would like to -- if that's not correct, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Karadzic said: We are going to send all of those who are capable of fighting. It was his sentence. And then I only confirmed that. It is Dr. Karadzic who actually said that they should be mobilised, the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that you instructed such mobilisation, but you were talking about people, and when Mr. Karadzic says "We'll mobilise them," if these would have been small children, I take it that you would have said it's impossible because they're small children.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, logically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, at least among them, if not all, were men of military age? Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not know about the composition of this group. But let me just explain this, Your Honour. This was a neighbourhood that was separated from Sarajevo. They did not have any contact. So when Serbs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm first putting my questions to you, and then if you would like to add something, you may do so. What now if a group of people, most likely including men of military age, if you would like to have them? And you say: I'll try to exchange them. How is this to be reconciled with your concern to give people a safe place and to protect them from war operations? What's the use of: "We'll try to exchange them." Why an exchange? You want military men, and you just told us that these Hadzici people at least included women and children. Why not let the women and children go and ask politely to have the men of military age to be sent to your -- the territory under your control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you understood this, Your Honour, I informed Radovan that it had been already seven days that no one wanted those people from Kula. I could not order my subordinates to send them to Sarajevo. Nobody wanted to receive them in the places where they wanted to go, that is to say, to the territory where the other side was in power. And these people didn't know what to do with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if you, in return, would ask for the military-aged men, at least a group including military-aged men from Hrasnica, then you thought the chances would be better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I tried to send them there to Hrasnica so that the local people, the government there in Hrasnica, would receive them. There were several governments there, locally. There was not a single government either on the Serb side or on the Muslim side. So no one wanted to listen to the other ones, and there wasn't any good coordination there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the core of my question is: Where you say -- let's -- let me put it very bluntly. I can't get rid of these women and children who need protection against war operations that lasts already seven days. Let me, in return to that, ask for some -- a group of people, among which military-able men, in return, and then you would expect that -- I mean, I'm trying to understand the logic of it. Would you then expect it, if you ask -- you would ask in return for the Hrasnica people, of which Mr. Karadzic said, "Let's mobilise them and let's" -- those fit for combat, what's the logic of having a better chance to, well, again, bluntly, to get rid of the women and children if you ask in return for military men, at least a group including military men, the expectation that they would be of any good for military purposes? I'm trying to understand the logic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I asked for my own family and neighbours from Hrasnica. They were probably Serbs who were of military age there as well. But what was the most important thing for me was to get this small group of people out of Hrasnica. They were detained there at the school, tortured, et cetera. So, in a way, if these people from Sarajevo didn't want to receive this group of people from Hadzici, less these people from Hrasnica take them in. Let them go anywhere. Just let's not keep them in the prison in Kula. Several times, people complained to me, people who were involved in exchanges. They would tell me that if people came from, say, Hadzici, Ilijas, Ilidza, Vogosca, where the Serbs controlled the territory, in Sarajevo, they simply did not want to take them in and these people could not get in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then you thought an offer to exchange them would have better chances; is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, do you recall how you determined that there were no more Croats in Kula? And I'm referring to a portion of your conversation with Dr. Karadzic that occurred just after that portion we've been discussing.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably up there in Pale or somewhere, Dr. Karadzic asked to have the Tomic brothers found, to be exchanged, to be returned to their families. I took this task seriously and I was looking for these people. I asked Tepavcevic or whoever else was down there whether they were on the lists and whether these people were in Kula. And they said no. Then I informed Dr. Karadzic about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And during -- I take it that during the course of that -- the effort you've just described, you were advised that there were no more Croats in Kula, or did you learn from some other effort?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I asked: Is Tomic there? And then the people who worked down there who were in charge of exchanges, they're either at a local level of the municipality of Ilidza or Sarajevo or the Central Commission, whatever, they told me that there was not a single ethnic Croat in prison, and this man was a Croat. Therefore, I knew that that man was not there either. Because I was not aware of who all the people in prison were before I would ask the chief of police, Tepavcevic, or one of the commanders who was here, and then they would report to me and inform me about who was there if I came on a specific assignment. The seat of the government was in Pale, or rather, in Jahorina, and I would come every now and then because of my work for the judiciary. And then, in addition to other things, I would do things for Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and others if they asked me to do something specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm looking at the clock. We're close to 7.00. Would this be a --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- suitable time to -- yes. A few procedural issues. It's no problem if the witness is still there. First of all, Mr. Tieger, Mr. Stewart more or less suggested that 443 might be the same as 411. I see no difference between the two of them. If there is any difference, please tell us. Otherwise, 443 should be not admitted, being the same document already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. And I thank Mr. Stewart for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the second issue: We have been confronted with some nasty translation problems in respect of P292, which had been admitted in evidence already. That was the issue about "did they leave" or -- three translations. We earlier had a similar problem with "they've already been transferred" or "are already crossing over there." The Chamber would very much like that you take care to review P292 very carefully, provide a translation without mistakes, preferably, so that it could replace P292.1 as the English translation of that telephone intercept. Then I draw the attention to the parties that we still have this issue of listening to the tape exactly, listening to the audiotape to find out exactly what the answer of the witness was, the issue whether it was "report" or "inform." You remember that. I'll ask the registrar to provide that portion of the tape. You will not have it available at this moment, because it's part of the same session where we went into an ex parte hearing. But would you please get in touch with the -- and both parties get in touch with the registrar to find out whether there's any need for corrections. Apart from that, we are close to the weekend, so although we are past 7.00 already, is there any issue, any procedural issue? I'm not inviting you, but just asking you whether there's any urgent procedural issue we have to address now. No. Then, Madam Registrar, we'll continue next Monday in Courtroom II, at 9.00. We adjourn until then. I have to apologise. I've forgotten to instruct you, Mr. Mandic, not to speak with anyone about your testimony still to be given or still about to be given. We are then now adjourned until next Monday morning, 9.00, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 29th day of November 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
